title: Ecological footprint

definition.text: A measure of how much nature, counted as biologically productive land and sea, people need to support their way of life and their economies.

facts.text: Footprint accounts compare the productive area people use for their consumption with the productive area actually available, called biocapacity.
It can be calculated for an activity, a person, a city, a nation or all of humanity, and split by consumption category such as food, housing and goods.
Resource use of every kind is converted into standard land areas called global hectares.
Global Footprint Network estimated humanity's footprint for 2023 at 1.71 planet Earths: demand 1.71 times what ecosystems renewed.
Humanity's footprint grew from 7.0 billion global hectares in 1961 to 20.6 billion in 2014, driven by higher use per person and more people.
The carbon footprint is the fastest-growing part, about 60% of humanity's total ecological footprint.
Per-person footprints range from 14.3 global hectares in Qatar to 0.5 in Yemen.
Mathis Wackernagel developed the concept and method as his PhD with supervisor William Rees in Vancouver from 1990 to 1994; Rees coined the name.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Ecological footprint by country

definition.text: Comparisons of national footprints that show how unequally countries use the planet's resources.

facts.text: A nation's total footprint is its footprint per person multiplied by its population.
In 2022 China had the largest total footprint, 5.54 billion global hectares, followed by the United States with 2.66 billion.
Plotting footprints against the Human Development Index shows that higher living standards generally tend to be less sustainable.
Footprints also vary widely within a country, with individual lifestyles and wealth.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Ecological footprint critiques

definition.text: The scholarly argument over whether the ecological footprint is a reliable and fair measure of human demand on nature.

facts.text: Critics and Global Footprint Network researchers wrote a joint paper setting out the terms of the controversy.
Government agencies that repeated the calculations largely confirmed the results, getting near-identical numbers.
Replacing old forests with high-yield plantations can raise measured biocapacity and so lower the footprint, a perverse result.
Some argue the measure has an anti-urban bias, making dense cities look "parasitic".

contested_note: Researchers have published critiques, replies and rejoinders on the method's reliability since 1999.
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Carbon footprint

definition.text: The total amount of greenhouse gases that an activity, product, company or country adds to the atmosphere, expressed as one comparable number.

facts.text: It is usually reported in tonnes of CO2-equivalent per unit, such as per year, per kilogram of protein or per kilometre travelled.
CO2-equivalent sums all greenhouse gases, not only carbon dioxide, into one figure.
It lets people compare the climate impact of individuals, products, companies and countries and set priorities for cutting it.
The World Bank put the global average in 2014 at about 5 tonnes of CO2 per person on a production basis.
With 9–10 billion people by 2050, a footprint of about 2–2.5 tonnes CO2e per person is needed to stay within a 2 °C target.
The term was first used in a BBC vegetarian food magazine in 1999.
Focusing on carbon alone can lead people to ignore or worsen other harms such as biodiversity loss and habitat destruction.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions
article: Carbon footprint#Types of greenhouse gas emissions

definition.text: The Greenhouse Gas Protocol's three-way split of an organization's emissions into direct ones, those from bought energy, and all other indirect ones in its value chain.

facts.text: Scope 1 covers emissions the organization causes directly, such as burning fuel on site; for a person, a car or gas stove.
Scope 2 covers indirect emissions from purchased electricity, heat, cooling or steam.
Scope 3 covers all other indirect emissions from sources the organization does not own or control, including suppliers and product users.
In 2022 about 30% of US companies reported Scope 3 emissions.
Footprints that leave out Scope 3 can mislead customers about the real footprint of companies or products.
Scope 1 covers direct emissions from sources a company owns or controls, such as its fuel and vehicles.
Scope 3 covers suppliers and product users; it made up 75% of emissions reported to the Carbon Disclosure Project.
Oil companies claiming net-zero operations leave out customers burning their oil, 70–90% of oil-related emissions, which falls in Scope 3.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Consumption-based emission accounting
article: Carbon footprint#Consumption-based emission accounting based on input-output analysis

definition.text: A way of counting a country's emissions that assigns all the emissions along a global supply chain to the place where the goods are finally consumed.

facts.text: Its opposite, production-based or territorial accounting, counts only emissions released inside the country and is what countries report to the UNFCCC.
Consumption-based accounting includes the emissions behind imported goods and services, so it is more comprehensive.
It rests on input-output analysis, extended worldwide as multi-regional input-output analysis (MRIO).
Consumption-based emissions reflect the lifestyle choices of a country's citizens.
Counting trade reverses the apparent fall in developed countries' emissions, turning a 2% decrease under production accounting into a 7% increase.
It is more complex and uncertain, since it needs an extra step and data from every trading partner; some suggest using it as a 'shadow' to production accounts.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Personal carbon footprint debate
article: Carbon footprint#Shifting responsibility from corporations to individuals

definition.text: The dispute over whether promoting personal carbon footprints shifts responsibility for climate change from fossil fuel companies to individuals.

facts.text: BP ran a large advertising campaign that helped popularize the personal carbon footprint.
Critics say many fossil fuel companies used this strategy to blame individual choices for their industries' harms.
The IPCC notes that individual behaviour changes alone cannot deliver deep emission cuts.

contested_note: Critics argue the concept was promoted to move blame onto consumers, while it remains widely used for personal choices.

conflicts.note: Other sentences on the same page date the BP/Ogilvy campaign to 2005 (S:43510061ec64, S:f3a35f7ce3d6).

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Carbon footprint of food

definition.text: The greenhouse gas emissions caused by producing a food, which differ greatly between plant-based foods and meat or dairy.

facts.text: 100 grams of protein from peas emits 0.4 kg CO2eq; the same protein from beef emits nearly 90 times more, 35 kgCO2eq.
Most of a food's footprint comes from the farm or land use change, little from transport and packaging, so what you eat matters more than food miles.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Sustainability metrics and indices

definition.text: Numerical measures that try to quantify the environmental, social and economic sides of sustainability.

facts.text: There is no universal standard, so disciplines and international organizations have proposed many different indicators.
Examples include the Ecological Footprint, the Human Development Index, the Genuine Progress Index and the Environmental Sustainability Index.
Such aggregate measures give a more detailed view of development than traditional indicators such as GDP.
Interest in Sustainable Development Index systems has expanded since the 2010s, more in industrialized than developing countries.
Although increasingly popular, sustainability indicators often have limited effect on actual policy and practice.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Daly rules
article: Sustainability metrics and indices#"Daly Rules" approach

definition.text: Herman Daly's three operating rules for ecological sustainability, covering renewable resources, nonrenewable resources and pollution.

facts.text: Renewable resources such as fish, soil and groundwater must be used no faster than they regenerate.
Nonrenewable resources such as minerals and fossil fuels must be used no faster than renewable substitutes can be put in place.
Pollution and wastes must be released no faster than natural systems can absorb, recycle or neutralize them.
Daly built on theory from Nicholas Georgescu-Roegen's 1971 book The Entropy Law and the Economic Process.
Some see the rules as the physical counterpart of the Brundtland definition, which supplies the ethical goal of not depleting natural capital.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Natural Step framework
article: Sustainability metrics and indices#Natural Step approach

definition.text: A science-based definition of sustainability, built by consensus after the Brundtland report, that sets out system conditions a sustainable society must meet.

facts.text: Swedish cancer scientist Karl-Henrik Robèrt coordinated the consensus process behind it.
A sustainable society does not keep raising concentrations of substances taken from the Earth's crust or made by society, does not degrade the environment, and lets people meet their needs.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Circles of Sustainability

definition.text: A framework for choosing sustainability indicators, organized around four domains: economics, ecology, politics and culture.

facts.text: Rather than prescribing indicators, it guides decisions about which indicators are most useful.
Each domain has seven sub-domains, each linked to indicators.
Agencies including the UN Global Compact Cities Programme have used it since 2010.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Emergy sustainability index
article: Sustainability metrics and indices#Energy, Emergy and Sustainability Index

definition.text: An index proposed by M.T. Brown and S. Ulgiati in 1997 that divides the emergy yield ratio by the environmental loading ratio.

facts.text: Emergy means embodied energy; Howard T. Odum coined the term and its accounting system in 1956.
The index accounts for yield, renewability and environmental load.
Leone notes that it calculates supply constraints that reporting schemes like the GRI do not.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Environmental Sustainability Index
article: Sustainability metrics and indices#Environmental Sustainability Index

definition.text: A country index of environmental sustainability built by Yale and Columbia University centres with the World Economic Forum and released in 2005.

facts.text: It was formally released at the World Economic Forum in Davos on 28 January 2005.
Its report compared it with other indicators such as the Ecological Footprint.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Earth Overshoot Day

definition.text: The calculated date each year on which humanity's use of resources passes what Earth can regenerate in that whole year.

facts.text: It equals world biocapacity divided by world ecological footprint, multiplied by the 365 days of the year.
In economic terms it is the day the planet's yearly regenerative budget is spent and humanity starts deficit spending.
Andrew Simms of the New Economics Foundation developed the idea; Global Footprint Network calculates it.
Human consumption began to outstrip what the planet could reproduce in the early 1970s.
In 2020 coronavirus lockdowns pushed the date to 22 August, more than three weeks later than 2019; in 2024 it fell on August 1.
Critics say it mainly reflects excess carbon dioxide and measures land and water mismanagement poorly; the Breakthrough Institute called it a publicity stunt.

contested_note: Critics argue the date mostly reflects carbon emissions, and Global Footprint Network researchers published a response.
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Water footprint

definition.text: The total volume of fresh water used to produce the goods and services that a person, community or business consumes or produces.

facts.text: Water use is counted as the volume evaporated or polluted per unit of time.
Arjen Hoekstra coined the concept in 2002 as a consumption-based indicator, analogous to the ecological footprint of the 1990s.
Unlike traditional withdrawal statistics, it shows where water is used and polluted, not only how much.
The average global water footprint of an individual is 1,385 m3 per year.
A product's footprint is the sum over all processes in its supply chain divided by the number of units.
ISO 14046:2014, issued in July 2014, gives guidance for water footprint assessments based on life-cycle assessment principles.
Critics note that a footprint means little without regional scarcity: 140 litres for a cup of coffee may be harmless in humid areas but damaging in arid ones.

distinct_from: Blue, green and grey water footprints
notes: S:869ab7f3c633 gives the 1996–2005 global water footprint as '9.087 billion m3/yr' but equates it to 9,087,000,000,000,000 litres; the unit looks wrong, so it is not used.
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Blue, green and grey water footprints

definition.text: The three parts of a water footprint: blue for surface and groundwater, green for rainwater, and grey for water needed to dilute pollution.

facts.text: A blue footprint counts water taken from lakes, rivers, wetlands and aquifers that evaporates, enters a product or is returned elsewhere or later.
A green footprint counts rain stored in the soil's root zone that plants transpire or take up; it matters most for farm and forest products.
A grey footprint is the water needed to dilute pollutants until the water meets agreed quality standards.
Green water has been estimated at 94% of the water footprint of global beef cattle production.
Critics say the grey footprint treats pollution like scarcity, though the two affect people and nature differently.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: National water footprint

definition.text: The water used to produce the goods and services consumed by a nation's inhabitants, wherever that water is used.

facts.text: The internal footprint uses domestic water; the external footprint is water used abroad to make imported goods.
It is calculated from domestic water use by subtracting virtual water exported and adding virtual water imported.
It shows that several countries rely heavily on foreign water, and such dependencies are likely to grow with trade liberalisation.

distinct_from: Blue, green and grey water footprints
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Biocapacity

definition.text: An estimate of how much an ecosystem can produce of useful biological materials and how much waste such as carbon dioxide it can absorb.

facts.text: It is the supply side that the ecological footprint is compared with to measure human impact.
In 2016 Earth had about 12.2 billion hectares of productive land and water; divided among 7.4 billion people, that is 1.6 global hectares per person.
Those 1.6 global hectares also include the space wild species need.
An area's biocapacity is its physical area multiplied by a yield factor and an equivalence factor.
It changes with technology, since what counts as a useful material can change from year to year.
Population growth can lower biocapacity per person, since Earth's resources must be shared among more people.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Biocapacity deficit

definition.text: The gap that opens when a population's ecological footprint is larger than the biocapacity of the area it lives in.

facts.text: A deficit comes from overusing one's own ecosystems, net imports, or use of the global commons.
A region whose biocapacity exceeds its footprint has a biocapacity reserve.
Using 1.7 Earths means a year's resource use takes one year and eight months to regenerate.
Carbon dioxide from burning fossil fuels is the dominant cause of global overshoot.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Global hectare

definition.text: The adjusted unit of footprint accounting: a hectare with the world's average biological productivity in a given year.

facts.text: It is needed because not all hectares produce the same amount of ecosystem services.
Footprint studies turn the use of energy, food, fibre, building materials and water into global hectares.
Wackernagel and Rees's early estimate of about 1.3 hectares per person was lower partly because those studies did not yet use global hectares.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Life-cycle assessment

definition.text: A method for adding up the environmental impacts of a product, process or service across every stage of its life, from raw materials to disposal.

facts.text: For a manufactured product it runs from extracting raw materials (cradle) through making, distributing and using it to recycling or disposal (grave).
An LCA inventories the energy and materials needed across the supply chain and calculates the resulting emissions.
It covers more than greenhouse gases, including water pollution, air pollution and ecotoxicity.
First used mainly to compare a product with alternatives, it is now used in product design, ecolabelling, consumer education and government policy.
An LCA is only as accurate as its data, which are either unit process data or environmental input-output data.
Critics note that not every factor can be reduced to a number, and rigid system boundaries make change hard to capture.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Phases of life-cycle assessment
article: Life-cycle assessment#Main ISO phases of LCA

definition.text: The four phases in which the ISO 14040 and 14044 standards say a life-cycle assessment is carried out: goal and scope, inventory, impact assessment and interpretation.

facts.text: Goal and scope set the product's function, the functional unit, the system boundaries, assumptions and allocation rules.
Life cycle inventory (LCI) quantifies raw material and energy needs and all emissions and releases over the product's life.
Life cycle impact assessment (LCIA) evaluates the potential environmental and human health impacts of those flows.
Interpretation summarizes the results and ends in conclusions and recommendations.
The phases are interdependent, so no stage counts as final until the whole study is done.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: LCA system boundaries

definition.text: The variants of life-cycle assessment that differ in which stretch of a product's life they cover, such as cradle-to-grave, cradle-to-gate and gate-to-gate.

facts.text: Cradle-to-grave covers the full life from resource extraction to disposal; cradle-to-gate stops at the factory gate and leaves out use and disposal.
Cradle-to-cradle is a cradle-to-grave assessment whose final step is recycling into new products.
Well-to-wheel is the variant used for transport fuels and vehicles.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Economic input–output life-cycle assessment
article: Life-cycle assessment#Economic input–output life cycle assessment

definition.text: A form of life-cycle assessment that uses sector-level data on each industry's environmental impact and its purchases from other industries.

facts.text: It captures long supply chains, such as cars needing energy and energy needing vehicles, easing the scoping problem of process LCA.
But it relies on sector averages that may not fit a specific product, and its translation of money into impacts is not validated.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Life cycle energy analysis

definition.text: An approach that counts all the energy a product needs, including the energy used to make its components, materials and services.

facts.text: Net energy content is a product's energy minus the energy used to extract and convert it.
A controversial early result claimed that making solar cells needed more energy than they recover.
Energy alone ignores whether flows are renewable and whether wastes are toxic.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Living Planet Index

definition.text: An indicator of the state of global biodiversity built from population trends of vertebrate species around the world.

facts.text: WWF developed it in 1997 with UNEP-WCMC; since 2006 the Zoological Society of London manages it with WWF.
As of 2022 it drew on 31,821 populations of 5,230 species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish.
The 2024 report showed monitored wildlife populations falling by an average of 73% between 1970 and 2020.
Declines averaged 94% in Latin America and the Caribbean; land-use change and habitat loss are a key driver.
It is limited to vertebrates because long-term data for invertebrates and plants are scarcer.
Media often wrongly report it as showing that 69% of all animals or species were lost since 1970.
Studies have found it sensitive to outliers and biased by its mathematics, possibly overstating declines.
It was used to measure progress toward the Convention on Biological Diversity's 2010 target and Aichi targets.

contested_note: Researchers dispute whether the index reflects true changes in abundance, with re-analyses suggesting it overstates declines and counter-critiques of those re-analyses.
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Sustainability measurement

definition.text: The frameworks and indicators used to measure how sustainable a process, product, service or business is.

facts.text: Sustainability is hard to quantify, perhaps impossible, because it has no fixed definition.
Frameworks look at environmental, social and economic domains, and the tools include indicators, benchmarks and audits.
The toolbox includes life-cycle assessment for resource use, the ecological footprint for consumption, and the Environmental Performance Index for governance.
The UN Commission on Sustainable Development published a list of 140 indicators covering environmental, social, economic and institutional aspects.
A benchmark is a reference point for a measurement; once set, it allows trends and progress to be measured.
Because each country uses its own indicators, global comparisons can be misread; common indexes would allow comparison.

distinct_from: Hubbert peak as a depletion metric
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Sustainability indicator
article: Sustainability measurement#Sustainability indicators and their function

definition.text: A measure that tracks some part of the interplay between the environment and social and economic activity, mainly to inform public policy.

facts.text: Indicator sets answer simple questions: what is happening (descriptive indicators), are we reaching targets (performance indicators), are we improving?
They are scientific constructs whose principal purpose is to inform public policy-making.
Indicators cover the environment, society or the economy, but there is no fixed definition of a sustainability indicator.

distinct_from: Hubbert peak as a depletion metric
part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Hubbert peak as a depletion metric

definition.text: The use of the Hubbert production curve, which rises to a peak and then declines, as a measure of how far a non-renewable resource has been depleted.

facts.text: A modified Hubbert curve applies to any resource harvested faster than it is replaced, such as an over-pumped aquifer.
Fisheries such as whaling and North Sea cod show that human pressure is pushing many resources through a Hubbert-like depletion cycle.
Phosphorus, essential to farming, is estimated to run out in 60 to 130 years.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: DPSIR framework

definition.text: A cause-and-effect framework that sorts information about a society–environment problem into drivers, pressures, state, impacts and responses.

facts.text: Drivers are social, demographic and economic developments, such as population growth, that lead to human activities affecting the environment.
Pressures, such as emissions or waste, change the state of the environment, which in turn has impacts on human well-being.
Responses are actions, mostly policy, that adjust drivers, reduce pressures, restore the state or soften impacts.
The European Environment Agency developed it in 1999, building on the OECD's 1993 Pressure-State-Response framework.
Critics say its categories are ill-defined: a wastewater plant is a response to pollution but a pressure when its effluent causes eutrophication.
It is also criticized for oversimplifying and for sidelining local and indigenous knowledge.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Ecological indicator

definition.text: A measure that sums up the state of an ecosystem, or the human impact on it, in simple terms for the public and policy makers.

facts.text: For example, the number of beetle taxa in a field can indicate its biodiversity.
They save cost and time: instead of counting every bird and plant in a restored wetland, a few indicator species can be monitored.
Ecological indicators are a subset of environmental indicators and refer only to ecological processes.
Limits include patchy data, no international standards, missing reference levels, and neglect of hard-to-measure values such as aesthetics.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Embedded emissions

definition.text: The greenhouse gases released in making a good, counted as belonging to whoever consumes it; also called embodied emissions or embodied carbon.

facts.text: The UNFCCC counts emissions where goods are produced, so emissions embedded in imports are attributed to the exporting country.
Choosing between production and consumption accounting is partly a question of equity: who is responsible for emissions.
Research found that in 2004, 23% of global emissions were embedded in internationally traded goods, flowing mostly from China and developing countries to the US, Europe and Japan.
Wang and Watson (2007) suggested nearly a quarter of China's CO2 emissions might come from producing exports.
In Western Europe imported emissions make up 20-50% of consumed emissions.
A carbon tariff or border carbon adjustment is a tariff on the carbon embedded in imports.
Emissions are usually counted where they are produced, as countries do when reporting to the UNFCCC.
A large share of CO2 emissions is traded internationally.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Embodied carbon in buildings

definition.text: The emissions from extracting, making, transporting and installing a building's materials, and from its repair and end-of-life treatment, as opposed to the emissions from running it.

facts.text: Studies estimate embodied carbon at 30% to 40% of global carbon emissions in the construction sector.
As buildings run more efficiently, embodied carbon's share of a building's life-cycle emissions has risen from about 20% to 50%.
Hence the saying "The greenest building is the building that is already built": re-use avoids large construction emissions.
It can be cut by using less material and substituting lower-carbon materials such as timber, bamboo or cement alternatives.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Top-down and bottom-up carbon accounting
article: Embedded emissions#Top-down, bottom-up and hybrid approaches

definition.text: The three main ways to quantify embodied carbon: bottom-up process-based LCA, top-down environmentally extended input-output models, and hybrids of the two.

facts.text: Bottom-up LCA can assess specific products but suffers truncation, because no study can follow the whole supply chain.
Top-down EEIO multiplies greenhouse gas intensity, such as tCO2e per dollar, by the final demand for each product.
EEIO's sector aggregation makes specific products hard to assess; hybrid methods combine both to reduce each one's weakness.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Emission intensity

definition.text: The amount of a pollutant released per unit of an activity, such as grams of CO2 per megajoule of energy or greenhouse gases per unit of GDP; also called carbon intensity.

facts.text: Intensities let analysts estimate emissions from activity data such as fuel burned, animals kept or distances travelled.
They also let people compare the environmental impact of different fuels or activities.
Carbon intensity per kilowatt-hour is widely used to compare sources of electricity.
Coal, mostly carbon, has a high CO2 intensity; natural gas, with four hydrogen atoms per carbon, has a medium one.
In Europe from 1990 to 2007, CO2 per unit of GDP fell by 2.3% a year, faster than energy intensity at 1.4% a year.
Different calculation methods, from full LCA to combustion-only, can give different results.
It is also called carbon intensity or emissions intensity.
The carbon intensity of global energy fell 13%, from 66.3 to 58.0 kg CO2/GJ, between 1978 and 2018, mainly through more renewables and nuclear.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Emission factor

definition.text: A fixed rate linking an activity to the emissions it causes, so that emissions equal activity multiplied by the emission factor.

facts.text: CO2 and SO2 from burning fuel can be estimated very precisely, because they depend almost entirely on the fuel's known carbon and sulphur content.
Other pollutants depend on combustion technology, so their factors are less certain.
A major use is in national greenhouse gas inventories reported to the UNFCCC, with IPCC Guidelines as the main source of default factors.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Lifecycle emissions of electricity sources

definition.text: The total greenhouse gases released per unit of electricity over the whole life of each kind of power plant, as compiled by the IPCC in 2011.

facts.text: Median values in g CO2-eq per kWh: hydroelectric reservoir 4, nuclear 16, solar PV 46.
Natural gas combined cycle without scrubbing emits 469 g per kWh and coal 1001.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Emission inventory

definition.text: An account of how much of one or more pollutants or greenhouse gases all sources in an area release over a set period, usually a year.

facts.text: Emissions are the starting point of every pollution problem, so inventories are needed to understand problems and track progress on them.
Each pollutant's emissions are usually estimated by multiplying each activity's level by an emission factor.
Countries report annual national inventories to the UNFCCC for greenhouse gases and to the LRTAP convention for air pollutants.
Facility-level reporting schemes such as Pollutant Release and Transfer Registers support public participation in decisions.
Scientists use inventories as inputs to air quality models, often needing finer spatial and time detail than national totals.
Greenhouse gas inventories also count removals by carbon sinks, unlike some other air emission inventories.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Emission inventory quality criteria

definition.text: The standards the UNFCCC and LRTAP conventions require of a national emission inventory: transparent, consistent, comparable, complete and accurate.

facts.text: Transparent means assumptions and methods are explained clearly enough for others to replicate the inventory.
Consistent means the same methods and data sets are used for the base year and all later years.
Accurate means estimates are systematically neither above nor below true emissions, with uncertainties reduced as far as practicable.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Environmental Performance Index

definition.text: A score that ranks countries on the environmental performance of their policies.

facts.text: It was started in 2002 by the World Economic Forum with Yale and Columbia University centres, and the report appears every two years.
The 2024 report uses 58 indicators to rank 180 countries on climate change mitigation, ecosystem vitality and environmental health.
In 2024 Estonia, Luxembourg, Germany, Finland and the United Kingdom ranked top, and India, Myanmar, Laos, Pakistan and Vietnam last.
Scores rise with national wealth, but with diminishing returns; rule of law and regulatory quality predict performance better than wealth.
Wealth funds clean water and waste management but also raises consumption, waste and emissions.
Critics fault its arbitrary choice of metrics and its bias against data-poor countries; India rejected its 176th place in 2024.

contested_note: Critics, including India's environment ministry, argue its indicators are arbitrary or biased; the index has since added and reweighted indicators.

conflicts.text: The 2024 index groups its 58 indicators into 11 issue categories.
conflicts.note: S:fa56d028d239 on the same page says the 58 indicators are grouped into 30 issue categories.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Environmental indicator

definition.text: A simple measure, tracked over time, that tells us what is happening in the environment.

facts.text: Indicators are a practical, cheaper way to follow a complex environment than recording every variable.
For example, the concentration of ozone-depleting substances in the air indicates the state of stratospheric ozone depletion.

Following the OECD's Pressure-State-Response model, there are state indicators, pressure indicators such as greenhouse gas emissions, and response indicators such as people served by sewage treatment.
Environmental indicators are a subset of sustainable development indicators, which also cover social and economic health.
Good indicators are judged on scientific credibility, policy relevance and practical data needs.
The public responds best to clear, simple indicators such as the UV index and air quality index.
Large indicator sets are condensed into indices, headline indicators, traffic-light visuals or dashboards.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Environmentally extended input–output analysis

definition.text: An environmental accounting tool that attaches resource use and emissions to an economy's input-output tables, so they can be traced through production to final consumption.

facts.text: It is the main way consumption-based accounts are compiled, as trade makes global resource use more important.
Each industry's extra inputs (energy, materials, labour) and outputs (emissions) are added as an extension matrix of factors per unit of output.
Multiplying final demand by the Leontief inverse and these factor coefficients allocates resource use and emissions to domestic or export demand.
National tables are combined into multi-regional input-output (MRIO) models to reflect differing production structures.
It assumes each industry makes one homogeneous product at one price, which aggregation and by-products violate.
It also assumes constant returns to scale, an assumption shared by life-cycle assessment.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Material footprint

definition.text: A consumption-based indicator of material use: all the raw materials needed along the supply chain to make the goods a country consumes, also called raw material equivalents.

facts.text: It counts direct and indirect flows, such as the ore mined for a phone's metal and the coal burned to power the refining.
It is comparable to carbon and water footprints, and is calculated with environmentally extended input-output analysis.
The total material footprint sums biomass, fossil fuels, metal ores and non-metal ores; it is an indicator for Sustainable Development Goals 8 and 12.
Material footprint per person rose 39 per cent from 2000 to 2017, reaching 12.18 tonnes.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Consumer and producer responsibility
article: Environmentally extended input–output analysis#Distributing environmental responsibility

definition.text: The choice of whether environmental impacts in input-output accounts are assigned to final consumers, to producers, or shared between them.

facts.text: Allocating all impacts to final consumers is consumer-based responsibility; allocating direct impacts to producers is production-based responsibility.
Hybrid schemes, including income-based ones and sharedness, have been proposed.
The importer gets the product, but the exporter gets the income, so how to share responsibility is unsettled.

contested_note: It has yet to be determined how responsibility for impacts embodied in exports should be shared between importing and exporting economies.

title: Waste input-output model
article: Environmentally extended input–output analysis#Waste and waste management

definition.text: An extension of environmentally extended input-output analysis by Nakamura and Kondo that tracks physical waste flows and their treatment alongside money flows.

facts.text: A simple waste footprint ignores that waste is usually treated into a less harmful form before recycling or disposal.
The model follows waste as treatment turns it into secondary waste and residues, through to recycling and final disposal.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Happy Planet Index

definition.text: An index, introduced by the New Economics Foundation in 2006, that measures how efficiently countries turn environmental impact into long, satisfied lives.

facts.text: Roughly, it multiplies life satisfaction by life expectancy and divides by the ecological footprint per person.
It was designed to challenge GDP and the Human Development Index, which are seen as ignoring sustainability.
Costa Rica led the 2009, 2012 and 2016 rankings and also the 2019 ranking, with a score of 62.1.
It is not a ranking of the happiest countries: the US, with high life satisfaction, ranked 108th.
Critics say it weights the footprint so heavily that the US would have needed a life expectancy of 439 years to match Vanuatu in 2006.
Data gaps forced estimates of footprint and life satisfaction for several countries.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: IUCN Red List

definition.text: The global inventory, founded in 1964, of the conservation status and extinction risk of the world's species.

facts.text: Its goals are to report species' status, draw attention to threatened biodiversity, and influence policy and conservation action.
As of 2023, 42,108 of 150,388 species surveyed were considered at risk of extinction from human activity such as overfishing, hunting and land development.
The IUCN aims to re-evaluate every species at least every ten years, through peer-reviewed specialist groups.
In 2012, 41% of amphibian species, 33% of reef-building corals, 25% of mammals and 13% of birds were threatened.
The first two volumes of Red Lists, for mammals and birds, were published in 1966.
A 2016 study argued its classification is inconsistent and that adding geospatial data would move many species to higher risk categories.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: IUCN Red List categories

definition.text: The nine groups into which the IUCN Red List sorts species, from Extinct to Not Evaluated, based on criteria such as rate of decline, population size and range.

facts.text: Extinct means beyond reasonable doubt no longer alive; Extinct in the Wild means surviving only in captivity or cultivation.
"Threatened" covers three categories: Critically Endangered, Endangered and Vulnerable.
Near Threatened, Least Concern, Data Deficient and Not Evaluated complete the scheme.
All new assessments since 2001 use version 3.1 of the categories and criteria.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: IUCN Red List of Ecosystems

definition.text: The IUCN's global framework for assessing and recording how close ecosystems are to collapse, the ecosystem-level counterpart of the Red List of species.

facts.text: It assesses biodiversity at a level of organization above species, replacing national protocols that were often not comparable.
The IUCN began developing it in 2008, finalized its categories and criteria in 2013, and officially recognized it in 2014.
It aims to evaluate all the world's ecosystems by 2025 to support conservation and resource management decisions.
It helps focus limited conservation effort on the ecosystems most likely to disappear.
Some countries, such as Finland, have adopted it as their official system for assessing ecosystem risk.
Critics point to the lack of a consistent way to classify ecosystems and to debate over the concept of ecosystem collapse.

contested_note: Its concepts, categories and criteria, especially ecosystem collapse, are debated.
distinct_from: Red List of Ecosystems categories and criteria

title: Red List of Ecosystems categories and criteria
article: IUCN Red List of Ecosystems#Categories and Criteria

definition.text: The eight risk categories and five criteria (A to E) the IUCN Red List of Ecosystems uses to rate an ecosystem's risk of collapse.

facts.text: Collapsed means the ecosystem's defining features and native biota are virtually certainly lost; only the Aral Sea and the Central Ayeyarwady palm savanna are so listed.
Unlike species extinction, ecosystem collapse is in theory reversible.
Formally, Critically Endangered means a 50% chance of collapse within 50 years, Endangered 20% within 50 years, and Vulnerable 10% within 100 years.
Criteria A and B measure spatial symptoms (declining or restricted distribution), C and D functional ones, and E models overall collapse risk.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Input–output model

definition.text: A quantitative economic model that shows how the sectors of an economy depend on one another, with each sector's output becoming other sectors' inputs.

facts.text: It is laid out as a matrix in which columns show the inputs each sector buys and rows show the outputs it sells, usually in money.
Wassily Leontief developed it and won the Nobel Prize in Economics for it; Quesnay's Tableau économique was a cruder forerunner.
Statistics offices use it in national accounts, including to calculate GDP.
It is increasingly used to quantify environmental footprints for consumption-based accounting, such as tracing embodied carbon between economies.
Being linear it is cheap to compute, but it needs huge amounts of data, so tables are often published 5–7 years late.
Because tables are in money, every dollar spent in a sector is assumed to cause the same damage, which can bias environmental estimates.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Leontief inverse

definition.text: The matrix (I−A)^−1 that turns final demand into the total output every sector must produce, counting all direct and indirect inputs.

facts.text: A technical coefficient is the amount of one good needed to make one unit of another.
In a two-sector coal and steel example, the economy must produce 19.19 units of coal to deliver only 7 to consumers.
The gap is indirect demand: coal to make steel and more coal, round after round, which the Leontief inverse sums.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Physical input-output table

definition.text: An input-output table measured in physical units instead of money, built to estimate environmental impacts more faithfully.

facts.text: Monetary tables must assume one price per good for the whole year and constant returns to scale.
Price does not track damage well: a $200 bottle of wine is unlikely to cause twenty times the impact of a $10 one.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Material input per unit of service
article: Material input per unit of service

definition.text: A measure of eco-efficiency, developed at the Wuppertal Institute in the 1990s, that divides the total material input of a product over its life by the units of service it provides.

facts.text: For a car, the service units are passenger kilometres over its life; less material per kilometre means a more eco-efficient car.
MIPS falls if less material is used or more service is delivered, for example by sharing a newspaper or a car, or making products last longer.
It counts five resource categories: abiotic, biotic, earth movements, water and air.
Its main weakness is that it ignores the toxicity of materials, so it should be used alongside other methods.

title: Ecological backpack
article: Material input per unit of service#Concept of ecological backpack

definition.text: The hidden material flows behind a product: its total material input minus the product's own weight.

facts.text: Backpacks are often many times heavier than the product itself.
Much of this material is moved in developing countries where raw materials are produced, while consumption happens mostly in the developed world.

title: Factor X
article: Material input per unit of service#Factor X concept

definition.text: Friedrich Schmidt-Bleek's idea of setting targets, such as Factor Four or Factor Ten, for dematerializing economies by raising resource productivity.

facts.text: It has been proposed that industrialized countries cut material flows by a factor of 10 to reach sustainable levels.
The Factor Ten Club, founded in 1994, and the Factor 10 Institute, founded in 1997, back the target.

title: Red List Index

definition.text: An indicator, built from the IUCN Red List, that tracks how the extinction risk of whole groups of species changes over time.

facts.text: Repeating conservation assessments at regular intervals lets changes in species' threat status reveal trends in extinction risk.
It can be broken down by taxonomic group, biogeographic realm, habitat type or main threat.
A sampled version (SRLI) assesses a representative sample of species, since assessing every fungus, insect and plant is impractical.
The shark and ray Red List Index has fallen 19% since the 1970s because of overfishing.
Australia's national bird RLI fell from 0.927 in 1990 to 0.896 in 2020, picking up both the 2019–2020 wildfires and conservation successes.
It is the single indicator for Sustainable Development Goal target 15.5 and was used for the CBD's 2010 biodiversity target.

part: Measuring wealth and accounting for nature

title: Human appropriation of net primary production

definition.text: An indicator, abbreviated HANPP, of how much of the plant growth that ecosystems produce each year is taken or prevented by human use, used as a proxy for human impact on nature.

facts.text: Josep Garí coined HANPP in 1996 and introduced it at the first conference of the European Society for Ecological Economics.
Land-use change has cut net primary production by 9.6% across the global land mass, and end consumption raises total HANPP to 23.8% of potential vegetation.
This share reduces the energy left for other species, affecting biodiversity, carbon and water flows, and ecosystem services.
The planetary boundaries framework uses HANPP to measure biosphere integrity.
